hypothesis: The neuron selectively responds to high-contrast, monochromatic (grayscale) imagery featuring richly textured surfaces defined by sharp tonal boundaries between bright white or light gray highlights and deep black or dark gray shadows. The activating visual features consist of detailed, organic or inorganic patterns—such as the coarse fur of animals, the striated feathers of birds, the pitted exoskeletons of insects, or the gleaming ridges of metallic objects—rendered exclusively in black and white. The neuron is invariant to semantic category (activating for biological subjects like dogs and birds as well as mechanical objects), scale, and perspective, provided the image lacks color and maintains strong local luminance contrast with distinct light-on-dark or dark-on-light polarity. The activating high-contrast textures typically dominate the composition, occupying approximately 30–80% of the image area and generally centering on the subject's primary surface details.
